performers: Lambert Murphy, tenor; Stefano Di Stefano, harp; William Carlino, lute
question: What changes when a medieval solo song is heard through a later accompanied arrangement?
intro: This complete acoustic record side pairs Machaut with Janequin in arrangements from Weckerlin’s collection. Murphy’s tenor, harp and lute document an early twentieth-century presentation of old French song, not an unaltered medieval performance.

sections.label: Paired songs · complete published side
sections.mNote: two arrangements retained together; their internal boundary is not aligned

cues.title: Two songs, one side
cues.text: This side contains Machaut’s Douce dame jolie and Janequin’s L’espoir que j’ai, in that order. Both pass through Weckerlin’s arrangements; the record is not a complete performance of Machaut’s original virelai.
cues.evidence: Victor label 45083-B numbers both songs and names Weckerlin’s Échos du temps passé. DAHR identifies the paired master B-15595. The analysis measures the whole side at 98.8 s but does not identify the switch between songs; no internal cut point is assigned.

cues.title: A name behind a pseudonym
cues.text: Victor also lists Lambert Murphy under the name Raymond Dixon. These are not two tenors sharing the side: DAHR identifies Dixon as Murphy’s pseudonym and credits the issued take to a single male soloist.
cues.evidence: DAHR B-15595 personnel explicitly says “Pseudonym for Lambert Murphy”; its description is male vocal solo with harp and lute. https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/matrix/refer/700000578

cues.title: Voice and plucked strings
cues.text: Across the side, compare the tenor’s sustained line with the shorter decay of the harp and lute. These accompaniments belong to this documented historical arrangement; they are not evidence for the instruments Machaut originally expected.
cues.evidence: The label specifies tenor with harp and lute; DAHR names Stefano Di Stefano for takes 3–4 and William Carlino. The report shows recorded sound continuing through this passage but cannot separate its instruments. No entrance, song boundary or original medieval instrumentation is inferred.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Lambert Murphy (tenor), Stefano Di Stefano (harp), William Carlino (lute)
fields.note: DAHR identifies Raymond Dixon as Murphy’s pseudonym, not a second singer. Di Stefano is credited for takes 3–4; Francis J. Lapitino belongs only to discarded takes 1–2 and is not credited on this issued take.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Two songs from J.-B. Weckerlin’s Échos du temps passé, volume I, performed with harp and lute
fields.note: The label numbers Machaut’s Douce dame jolie first and Janequin’s L’espoir que j’ai second; DAHR quotes the collection title and volume from Victor’s ledgers. BnF describes the published collection as voice with piano, so the precise harp-and-lute adaptation is not established from that score.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: Take 4 was made on 17 March 1915. The earlier matrix date 14 January 1915 refers to destroyed takes 1–2, not the recording streamed here.

fields.label: Place
fields.value: New York, New York, United States
fields.note: DAHR specifies New York for takes 3–4. Camden belongs to the January takes and is not substituted for this session; the studio address is unknown.

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Victor Talking Machine Company; blue label
fields.note: The viewed label names Victor and Lambert Murphy and specifies tenor with harp and lute, in French.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The side suffix B is visible on the label. LOC and DAHR identify the 10-inch carrier.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: DAHR marks take 4 as Master and links the same audio. Matrix/take identification comes from discographic records, not from claiming to read an illegible run-out inscription.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.value: Source disc: UCSB Davidson Library, Department of Special Collections; National Jukebox digital access; Hessel Digital Library mirror
fields.note: LOC identifies the source collection. The mirror credits digitisation to the Library of Congress Packard Campus; DAHR also describes the audio as from the UCSB Library. No individual transfer engineer is established.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The original disc-transfer date is unknown. The Archive mirror states LOC retrieval on 30 September 2026 and repository publication on 10 October 2026; neither is the 1915 session or 1916 release.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Archive describes its MP3 as a bit-exact copy of the LOC-served MP3, with no processing
fields.note: This records the mirror’s provenance statement, not an independently performed checksum comparison. Original stylus, speed correction, equalisation and noise-reduction settings are unknown. No additional audio cut is made.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Historical songs and Weckerlin collection are outside ordinary composition copyright terms
fields.note: BnF gives Weckerlin’s dates 1821–1910 and the collection’s publication in 1853–1857. The exact person responsible for adapting its piano accompaniment to harp and lute is not established. Recording admission rests independently on the documented pre-cutoff publication.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 2 — United States public domain: published May 1916
fields.note: Victor 45083’s documented 1916 publication precedes the project’s 1925 cutoff. source.rights uses us-published-before-cutoff with published 1916. The Archive Public Domain Mark is corroborative, not the sole basis; its 1915 first-publication claim and simplified statutory explanation are not repeated. This is a US basis, not a claim of worldwide clearance.
